bracket: [Textbook answer-key error (sign): the printed key gives the gravitational potential at the midpoint as \(2.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\) with no leading minus. With the zero of potential taken at infinity — the convention this chapter uses throughout — a gravitational potential is necessarily NEGATIVE, so the value is \(-2.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{J kg}^{-1}\). The magnitude, the zero field and the "unstable" verdict all agree with the key. It is not a dropped glyph: the same key entry prints a minus inside \(10^{-8}\), and the chapter's own table defines the potential as \(-GM/r\) while its Example 7.3 prints \(-4\sqrt{2}\,Gm/l\).]

[Textbook misprint in the book's own solution: its final line gives the change in potential energy as \(\Delta V = -6.25 \times 10^{9}\,\text{J}\); the sign should be POSITIVE. The book contradicts itself two lines earlier — the total energy change it prints requires \(\Delta K + \Delta V\) to give \(+3.12 \times 10^{9}\,\text{J}\), and \(-3.13 + 6.25 = +3.12\) works while \(-3.13 - 6.25 = -9.37\) does not. The printed \(-6.25 \times 10^{9}\,\text{J}\) is numerically the final potential energy itself, which is the likely origin of the slip. Raising a satellite's orbit RAISES its potential energy.]
